nameStory: Alpine sweetvetch gets its name from its sweet-tasting roots and its love of high, cold places - though in New England you'll find it in northern bogs rather than true alpine zones. Indigenous peoples of the Arctic have long called it 'Eskimo potato' because the starchy roots can be eaten like potatoes, and it's known as 'masu' in the Iñupiaq language.
description: Alpine sweetvetch is a hardy perennial herb that brings a splash of northern wilderness to New England's coldest corners. This member of the pea family produces spikes of bright pink to purple flowers that look like tiny snapdragons clustered together on stems that can reach 1-3 feet tall. The whole plant has a robust, almost shrubby appearance with compound leaves made up of oval leaflets, and it forms small colonies through underground runners.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink to purple pea-like flowers arranged in dense, elongated clusters at stem tips. Each individual flower has the classic legume shape with a banner petal on top, and the whole spike feels sturdy and substantial when gently touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-15 oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem, plus one at the tip. The leaflets feel smooth and somewhat thick, with a blue-green color that stands out against bog vegetation.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple sturdy stems arising from deep, thick roots. The whole plant has a robust appearance that looks almost out of place in delicate bog settings.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces flattened, segmented seed pods that break apart into individual sections when mature. The pods have a papery feel and often persist into fall, rattling softly in the wind.

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy taproot that can extend deep into the ground and has a slightly sweet taste when chewed raw - though always verify identification before tasting any wild plant.

habitat: This arctic wanderer finds refuge in New England's coldest, wettest places - primarily northern bogs, fens, and wet meadows in Vermont, New Hampshire, and northern Maine. Look for it in calcium-rich wetlands where cold groundwater seeps to the surface, often growing alongside sedges, wild mint, and other cold-loving plants. It needs consistently moist, cool conditions and is usually found at elevations above 1,000 feet.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges late in spring as compound leaves unfurl from thick underground roots. The plant builds its leafy framework slowly in the cool conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer (July-August) when the striking pink-purple flower spikes are most prominent. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and segmented seed pods develop, often persisting and turning brown. Leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant above ground, but the thick taproot survives frozen conditions that would kill most plants. Only dead stems may be visible above snow.

funFact: This plant is so tough it can survive being completely frozen solid for months - and its roots are so nutritious that they sustained Arctic explorer families through entire winters, earning it the nickname 'bear root' because even hungry bears dig them up as a crucial food source.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other bog plants like wild bergamot or marsh pea, but alpine sweetvetch's thick, robust stems and densely packed flower spikes set it apart. Remember: if it looks surprisingly sturdy and well-fed for a bog plant, with bright pink flower towers, you've probably found sweetvetch.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'alpine' sweetvetch, this plant isn't restricted to true alpine zones - it's actually more of a circumpolar species that thrives in any cold, wet environment. In New England, it represents a fascinating remnant of ice age flora that once covered much more territory when glaciers were retreating.
compareHints: Alpine sweetvetch is the only Hedysarum species found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other legumes in our region like wild lupine or beach pea, sweetvetch stands out with its much more robust appearance, thicker stems, and preference for cold, wet habitats rather than dry sandy areas. Its flower clusters are also much denser and more cylindrical than the loose racemes of most other regional legumes.
